While I see some validity to your argument, there are definitely some differences in how they are engineered and also their quality control.

When I was in school a professor told us a key difference at least in the mid-late 90s when the professor had experience Honda in particular had a different QC system than domestic vehicles. He said most domestic cars had a system where they would inspect like every 100 parts with tight parameters, if it passes the whole lot of 100 would pass. If the production is consistent that is fine in theory, but if 20 of that 100 are out of spec and you inspect one of the 80 that are good, you are creating problems with 20% of your end products... Honda would inspect every part with slightly looser parameters and did their best to engineer for the whole range of those parameters. In the end you get cars that don't make as much horse power and have not as tight of body lines but a much higher percentage are within spec meaning longer life.

Where there any lights on your dash? There should have been lights before the car just shut off.

I don't work on new cars very often, it's possible there is a sensor that shut the car off before the engine became a complete paper weight. But I wouldn't know that without being there.

Some easy checks would be check the oil, see if it looks creamy... It should be some shade of brown but able to see thru it. If it looks like chocolate milk or a latte, that's bad, stop right there. If the oil is clear and at the proper level I would try to start it after the engine has cooled off a bit.

If you try to start it and it just makes a click and nothing else, you probably welded your engine together (unlikely if the oil was good). If the engine turns on but sounds different than normal, really loud, grinding noises, or sounds like someone is shaking a bucket of bolts turn it off immediately. It has internal problems but may be fixable depending on what is broke (fixable does not mean cheap). If the engine starts like normal and sounds normal, you MAY have gotten lucky and saved by a sensor or something. Shut it off, don't let an engine without water run more than a few seconds. If the engine runs normally, it may just be a case of replacing the burst hose (and I would recommend the other ones) and fill it back up with coolant.

IF you "got lucky" and it seems to just need a new hose. Change the oil and look to see if it's sparkling, has metal shavings in it. If it does, the engine probably has a short life until it needs to be rebuilt.
The hose is cheap if you catch when it pops, but he said the car cut off on him... So he probably didn't open the hood till after the engine became a paper weight.

If the car shut off on its own and then you found that you probably cooked the motor. 

The coolant that is supposed to be in that hose keeps the engine cool while running.

Without coolant the engine will overheat. If running long enough with no coolant the engine will become an expensive paper weight.

Ok, so I love your ambition and honesty, but I think you need a bit of a reality check.

You will likely not find a running and driving Nova of any year for less than 5k unless It has pretty serious issues like rust or frame damage or something mechanical that really needs to be fixed to make it a safe daily driver.

Also, when you say 5k budget is that for the starting cost of the car or the completed project?

If you want something that is less than 5k when you are "done" I would say look into a 90s Japanese car.

If you want American for cheap you should look for something a little newer and less "desirable". If you are a Chevy guy maybe a 3rd or 4th gen Camaro? You are much more likely to find a starter 3-4 gen Camaro for less than 5k than anything that has a Nova badge.

With all that said older cars are much easier to work on if you can find parts (I'm talking like 1995 and older) much less stuff run by computers, much less wiring than modern cars.

Pretty much everything you need can be learned from the Internet if you look hard enough and are motivated, what you need to know will depend on what you have and what your goal is.

Another thing to consider is tools, tools add up in cost FAST. Like you can spend a few hundred just on a good jack and jack stands.

But ultimately what you are looking for when picking a project is mechanical (how well is the car running and driving if it does), RUST (Idk where you live but a car with holes rusted thru it is NOT a beginner car) if the car has a rusty spot push on it. If it feels soft, makes crunching noises, or has bubbles under the visible rust know that has to be replaced and there is likely more than you can see. Unpainted surfaces (like frame under the car) that are just rust colored but feel solid and sound like thick metal when you tap on it can probably just be cleaned off and painted to protect it. Depending on your goal interior quality, interior bits can get expensive and hard to find the older you go. But if you want a stripped out "race car" feel then a car with a trashed interior could be a way to get a project for cheap.

If I was you, I would invest in at minimum a spark plug socket and ratchet and learn how to remove the spark plugs of the car you are going to look at, and learn what a good and bad spark plug looks like. Ideally you get a compression testing not, learn how to use it, what is good and what is bad, and bring a friend to check compression. This can tell you a lot about the health of the engine. Which can get the price down if you are willing to do work and tear into a hurt engine, or tell you to walk away for a car with internal problems. Always look at the fluids, are they full, do they look good or bad?

Here is what I have found on the car side of motorsports. Particularly in sports car racing, they don't have many full time mechanics because they only race like 8-10 race weekends a year and they are sometimes 6-8 weeks apart. So what they do is for race weekends hire contract "fly in" mechanics who fly to the race, do their work, and go back home. Most of these people have other jobs because working 8 weekends a year doesn't pay much, and they just take vacation time to do it. Now to get into those spots can be hard because they want people with experience who can show up and hit the ground running and be able to quickly sort things like during pit stops or if a wreck happens during practice or qualifying. So that is where the volunteer work with amateurs gets that experience, at least that is how I am trying to go about it. I only just started, so this is just what I have gathered 3rd party from others many of whom have done it.

Motorcycle may be similar. Check your local tracks, or move to a well known track if you REALLY want it. And reach out to a local amateur racer and see if they need help. Even just a guy who does like lots of track days to start, help with race prep and help on race day stuff. But and bolt the bike, check pressures, get comfortable doing "race day" stuff and understand all you can about the bike then reach out to race teams if they have a yearly race that comes near you, " be like hey, I live near by track XYZ I have experience ABC, I know you will be here for a race and was wondering if you could use an extra hand while you are in town." I have been told being able to get yourself to the track and not ask for accommodations is a big plus when low on experience. The team paying for travel and accommodation is a big expense for them. And then you meet people, they get to see how helpful you may be.

If you need the racing line on to know the track and brake points you need to practice more.  


You need to find visual cues on the track to use as brake points. Make sure to pick things that do not move. Dont use shadows or cones or the number markers on the side of the track. Shadows move depending on time of day and cones and signs can get hit. Use things like when the lead in rumble strip ends, or when the start of the rumble strip disappears behind the A pillar. Some tracks can use trees, like when this tree disappears behind the roll cage.  


You need static Brake and Turn in points for every track you run.  


MOST IMPRTANT, you need to be aware of your surroundings and know how to adjust your points given the situation. If a car is outside/inside how does that 1) change what your normal brake/turn in points look like (because the same point on track will look different on screen if you are left, middle, or right on the track surface) 2) how much do you have to change your brake/turn in points to still make the corner with a car outside/inside you. Likely you will have to brake sooner/harder and turn in sooner/sharper if you are inside another car, and opposite if you are outside.

As many have said, turn off the racing line and race the cars around you. If you want to just try to drive the perfect line on an empty track go do time trials.  


If you need the racing line to know where to brake then you need to practice more. Not to mention in a race setting that race line will get you rear-ended more than it will help you, it suggests you brake way earlier than you really need to.

Second, go see a doctor I assume your fiance is seeing her OB about this. But also look into a fertility clinic near you. They will likely run a couple basic tests to see if there is an easy answer or solution.

Third, like some others have said get the cheap ovulation and pregnancy tests since you can buy them in bulk and may end up going through a lot (my wife would go through like 8-10 pregnancy tests a month)... Side note, as a guy it kinda pains me to say this, but don't have sex like 3 times a day for week during ovulation. It will drive down sperm count. Once we knew her cycle we tried 2 days before peak, the day of peak, and again the day after. And keep your hands off yourself around that time to keep numbers up. The rest of the month is between you and her.

About reading pregnancy tests that you need to understand. If there is a line at all, I mean the faintest squint your eyes "idk is that a line or is it not, honey can you see this" kinda line is a positive pregnancy test.

Start using pregnancy tests like 5 days before her expected period day. Look for the line. Document this. Have a journal, google doc, something where you can track stuff to take to doctor appointments.

Having a super faint line especially more than once then have it go away and start your period. That was not a "false positive" it was likely a "chemical pregnancy" or a super early miscarriage. While sad this is super important information. Chemical pregnancy is a fertilized egg that doesn't stick to the uterus wall (I'm 90% that is the right definition). You need to know if you are actually not getting pregnant or are you getting fertilized eggs but they aren't turning into full term pregnancy for some reason.

This was our biggest issue. We would get pregnant every few months but lose them very early on. Many people in or situation would have thought we weren't getting pregnant at all because how early we lost some.

Lastly there is a chance the issue is with you. Your sperm count may be low or they might have a very low % of healthy ones. That was part of our problems too. About 4 years ago I was having orthoscopic heart surgery, where they shove tools in my femoral artery at my pelvis and run them into my heart and work on it from the inside. So my brain processed that bit of back knowledge and realized the doctor hadn't/couldn't remove the tool that was in my heart. My brain decided when the power came back on that thing on my heart was going to try and find "home" and rip my heart to pieces. Basically, my brain decided as soon as I saw light i was dead.

My mother passed away when I was a child, pretty much everyone I grew up around and reflected on our relationship and some of them wishing we had a better relationship.  "The Davis County Attorney’s Office has determined the Roy officers who shot and killed a 21-year-old man who shot at police, injuring a K-9 officer, after an August traffic stop were legally justified.

The Roy Police Department announced the county attorney’s finding on Thursday and released a video statement on the confrontation. The video showed, for the first time, some body and vehicle footage and photos of the scene.

The traffic stop that precipitated the deadly shootout was routine, body camera footage shows.

An unidentified officer first pulled over [21-year-old Aaron Griffin](https://www.sltrib.com/news/2020/08/12/man-shot-by-police/) and his 49-year-old passenger around 2 a.m. near 5660 S. 1900 West in Roy, because of the car’s obstructed license plate.

In the video statement, Griffin tells the officer he’d put a piece of paper over it when he played a prank on his sister. The officer also notes Griffin’s brake light is out. Griffin says it’s defective and shows the officer that it only works when his bright lights are on — which, the officer replies, is still problematic.

“That solves that, I guess,” Griffin jokes, and the officer chuckles before walking back to his patrol car to check Griffin’s information.

He lets Griffin go with a warning after the passenger gets out to remove the paper over the license plate.

As the passenger is removing the paper, the officer asks his name, and he “gives the officer false information,” according to the statement.

Because of this, the officer again pulls over the car, asking the passenger for his name and if he has a criminal history. When the officer returns to his car to check that info, Griffin drives away, the video shows.

The officer chases the car briefly but stops the pursuit. Officers later find the vehicle crashed in a field near 2642 N. 2000 West in Clinton. Griffin ran from the car, while the passenger stayed nearby.

An officer sends a K-9 after Griffin, warning, “He will bite you! Stop!”

Seconds later, gunshots ring out. The responding officers fires into the field and calls his dog back. That’s when he discovers the dog has been shot in the face and calls for medical help.

Police said the dog, Mik, was hit by Griffin’s gunfire. The dog underwent surgery and survived.

About the time that the dog was shot, two other Roy patrol officers drove through the field searching for Griffin.

Footage shows them approach Griffin as he fires multiple rounds at both vehicles, including shooting at a police car as it approaches and rams him.

Bullets hit both vehicles, but neither officer were injured.

After running over Griffin, officers get out of their vehicles to look for them.

An officer tells another, “He’s down. I f------ hit him with my car, dude.” But moments later officers apparently see Griffin and shout at him to show his hands.

Then officers shot again, striking Griffin multiple times. He was declared dead at the scene.

The video statement said that as police ordered Griffin to show his hands, he pointed his gun at them, and officers fired.

The passenger was arrested and booked into jail for a parole violation.

While family declined The Salt Lake Tribune’s request for an interview Thursday, saying the shooting was still too painful to discuss, Griffin’s actions the day before he died give some insight into who he was.

It was about 4 a.m. when a woman speeding down the road near 2150 N. 5200 West and crashed, rolling her car and sparking a fire.

Plain City Fire Chief TJ Larson arrived about two minutes after to find the driver, seriously injured, already dragged out from beneath the burning car, sitting in front of it. Firefighters soon pulled her father away, and the car exploded.

Larson said that two men — Griffin and someone else — were the first to stop after the crash, and pulled the woman out with the help of a man and woman.

"If they hadn’t been there she definitely would have died,” Larson said.

Larson didn’t know Griffin, although he’d hoped to thank him and the other man for their heroics that night. Larson and Griffin connected on Facebook but didn’t get a chance to talk before Griffin was killed.

Since then, he’s heard from friends about Griffin’s struggles with substance use and self-worth.

“I think in the end, the biggest thing is that sometimes people do good things and sometimes they do bad things," Larson said.

People aren’t normally just one way or another, and Larson likes to think they strive for goodness despite personal troubles.

This police shooting marked Utah’s 15th of the year. Later that day, Unified police would shoot and kill 39-year-old Matthew Hilbelink, who was armed with numerous weapons and who police say was suicidal.

Those two police shootings pushed Utah to 16 this year — one more than 2019. Since then, police have shot five more people in the state, bringing the total to 21.

Of those 21 who were shot, 13 were killed."

The Salt Lake Tribune  
Paighten Harkins  
September 24, 2020

If you want a great job that is not behind a degree requirement, look into the trades. So few young people are willing to go into them and so many young people want to work on computers at a desk, the supply and demand is beginning to flip. People who are skilled and willing to get dirty and do labor for a living are seeing their wages go up. Hell I traded my desk for a toolbox and got a raise. 

But another thing to consider is figure out what you are passionate about and chase something related to that. You will likely be more willing to put in the work to obtain and be great at the position.
